solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Piratical Scottish writer with aural pendant, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly tells us the phrase before it is to be heard spoken rather than read

parts.note: John Buchan was a Scottish novelist; an aural pendant is an earring, hanging from the ear

explanation.surface: A puzzling description of a Scottish author sporting a dangly earring, like a pirate.
explanation.walkthrough: John Buchan wrote The Thirty-Nine Steps. Said quickly, 'Buchan earring' gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Buccaneers were pirates, so their raiding and plundering is piratical behaviour.

clue.text: Skating facility shortly opening by sea

indicators.note: the shortened rink sits in the middle of the word by, opening it up

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: shortly says to cut the last letter off the word for the skating facility

parts.note: an ice rink is where people skate

explanation.surface: An ice rink is about to open next to the seaside.
explanation.definitionFit: The briny is an informal name for the sea, from its salty water.

clue.text: Winning position of pal from Prague, do we hear?

indicators.note: the question asks whether we are hearing the phrase spoken aloud

parts.note: a friend from the Czech capital is a Czech mate

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a friend from Prague has reached a winning position, perhaps at chess.
explanation.walkthrough: Prague is the capital of the Czech Republic, and a mate is a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess, a king that is attacked and cannot escape gives the attacking player a win.

clue.text: Like some mines? Not near Pilsen, oddly

indicators.note: oddly suggests the letters of the phrase before it are arranged in a strange way

explanation.surface: A question about mines that, strangely, are not located near the Czech city of Pilsen.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipersonnel mines are designed to kill or injure people rather than destroy vehicles.

clue.text: Chap involved in noted war drama

indicators.note: involved in says the name is contained within the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A man is taking part in a celebrated play about war.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's name, standing for any male person or fellow.

clue.text: Mention where socks are kept — and instruction from bank?

parts.note: to mention something is to refer to it
socks are usually kept in a chest's drawer

explanation.surface: Someone mentions their sock drawer, and the bank sends a curt note.
explanation.walkthrough: A cheque's drawer is the person who writes it; British banks mark unpaid cheques with this phrase, sending the payee back to them.
explanation.definitionFit: The formula a bank writes on a bounced cheque, telling the payee to consult its writer.

clue.text: Disappointing score on field, regularly!

indicators.note: regularly says to take every second letter of the words before it

explanation.surface: A team scores nothing on the pitch, as so often happens.
explanation.definitionFit: A score of zero, as in a football result, is usually a letdown.

clue.text: Advantage, securing Nanny's initial approval

indicators.note: securing means holding the other piece firmly inside

parts.note: an asset is something useful, an advantage

indicators.note: initial points to the first letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: An advantage obtained once the nanny gives her first approval.
explanation.definitionFit: Agreement or permission given to a proposal is consent or approval.

clue.text: Popular record, but ultimately unskilful

parts.note: something popular is in fashion, or in
an EP is an extended-play record

indicators.note: ultimately points to the last letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A hit record that turns out to be poorly made after all.
explanation.definitionFit: Clumsy and lacking skill are the same thing; the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Cakes made by females in part of UK

indicators.note: in places the females within the part of the UK

parts.note: Wales is one of the four nations of the United Kingdom
F is the abbreviation for female, doubled here for the plural

explanation.surface: Cakes baked by women in one of the UK's nations.
explanation.definitionFit: Waffles are batter cakes cooked in a patterned iron, so they are a kind of cake.

clue.text: Asian ox tossing a girl over?

indicators.note: over says the girl's name is turned head over heels and read backwards

parts.note: Kay is a girl's name

explanation.surface: An absurd question: does the Asian ox toss a girl over its head?
explanation.definitionFit: The yak is a long-haired ox of the Himalayas and Tibet.

clue.text: Game bird pig trader shot

indicators.note: shot means ruined or broken, so the letters before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A game bird shot by a pig trader, or a trader of pigs shooting game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' looks like the bird's fate; it is the anagram signal on PIG TRADER.
explanation.definitionFit: This plump bird is shot for sport and food, so it is a game bird.

clue.text: Gloomy about one's son's sacking

indicators.note: about means placed around the other pieces

parts.note: dismal means gloomy
one is I, and one's gives I'S, here IS
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: Someone is gloomy about their son being sacked.
explanation.definitionFit: Being fired from a job is a dismissal, another word for a sacking.

clue.text: Position of professor, one tucking into tea

indicators.note: tucking into means going inside the other piece

parts.note: char is British slang for tea
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A professor eating during teatime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tucking into' looks like eating, but it means going inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A professorship is called a chair, the post held at a university.

clue.text: Commander's telly, oddly expensive

parts.note: CO is commanding officer, so a commander's is CO'S

indicators.note: oddly says to take the odd-numbered letters of the word before it

explanation.surface: The commanding officer's television is strangely pricey.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that costs a lot is pricey, i.e. expensive.

clue.text: Assault at filming location

definitions.meaning: an attack, especially the first rush of one
where cameras roll on a film, on the film set

explanation.surface: An attack takes place where a film is being shot.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means an attack or beginning, and split into two words means being at the film set.

clue.text: Person robbing bar, primarily desiring wine

parts.note: to bar something is to ban it

indicators.note: primarily points to the first letter of the word before it

parts.note: It is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and It

explanation.surface: Someone robs a bar mainly because they want wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Person robbing bar' reads as one phrase; the definition stops at 'robbing'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandit is an outlaw who robs, typically a highwayman or brigand.

clue.text: Prehistoric lizard gets knocked back by a sour concoction

indicators.note: knocked back means turned around, so the word is read backwards
a concoction is a mixture, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: Someone drinks a sour mixed drink, knocking it back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked back' reverses GETS to STEG; 'concoction' rearranges A SOUR into OSAUR.
explanation.definitionFit: This plated dinosaur's name means roofed lizard, an extinct reptile of the Jurassic.

clue.text: Where we may eat out? Not by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it says the word is heard spoken, not seen written

parts.note: not out is in

explanation.surface: Someone asks where to dine out, and seems to answer no.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eat out' feels like one phrase; 'out' belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub or inn serves meals, so it is a place to eat.

clue.text: Deprived journalist housed by Napoleonic marshal

indicators.note: housed by means placed inside the other piece

parts.note: Michel Ney was one of Napoleon's marshals
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A poor journalist given lodging by one of Napoleon's marshals.
explanation.definitionFit: Deprived people lack the basics of life, so they are poor and in want.

clue.text: Erudite English composer in the outskirts of Leatherhead

indicators.note: in places the pieces inside the outer letters
the outskirts of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: Thomas Arne composed Rule, Britannia!

explanation.surface: A learned English composer living on the edge of Leatherhead, a Surrey town.
explanation.definitionFit: Erudite people have much knowledge gained by study, so they are scholarly.

clue.text: A couple of points making us bristle!

parts.note: W and N are two compass points, west and north

explanation.surface: Two scored points make us bristle with anger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bristle' reads as a verb of anger; it is the noun for a hair on grass.
explanation.definitionFit: The awn is the stiff bristle on an ear of barley or other grass.

clue.text: Rubbish used to be tipped extensively, to begin with

parts.note: was is the past of be, so what used to be was

indicators.note: to begin with points to the first letters of the words before it

explanation.surface: Rubbish that was once dumped widely at a tip.
explanation.definitionFit: Refuse or garbage that is thrown away is the same as rubbish.

clue.text: Oxford, say, delayed mass meeting on own initiative

parts.note: Oxford is an example of a university, uni for short
something delayed is late
a rally is a mass meeting

explanation.surface: Oxford University held a late mass meeting on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting by one side alone, without the agreement of others, is acting on one's own initiative.
